ai.literal: He who says he desires freedom from contempt, let him guard his own mind against stealing even a single thing of whatever small measure.
ai.translation: He who wishes not to be despised by others must guard his own mind against the thought of stealing anything, however small.
ai.modern: பிறரால் இகழப்படாமல் வாழ விரும்புகிறேன் என்று சொல்பவன், எந்த ஒரு சிறிய பொருளையும் திருட நினைக்காதவாறு தன் நெஞ்சைக் காத்துக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that self-respect and avoiding the scorn of others begin with mental discipline. If a person desires to live without being looked down upon, they must protect their mind from even the slightest thought of theft. The word 'eḷḷāmai' refers to the state of not being despised, and 'kaḷḷāmai' refers to non-stealing. The poet emphasizes that even a tiny, hidden desire to take what belongs to another can ruin one's honor, so the mind itself must be guarded.

ai.literal: Even thinking by the mind is indeed evil, thinking 'we will steal another's property by deceit'.
ai.translation: Even to think in one's mind, 'We will steal another's property by deceit,' is evil.
ai.modern: பிறருடைய பொருளை வஞ்சனையால் திருடுவோம் என்று மனதால் நினைப்பது கூடத் தீமையானதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that the virtue of non-stealing begins in the mind. The author states that even the mere thought of taking another person's property through deceitful means is itself a sinful act. The word 'uḷḷattāl' refers to the mind, and 'uḷḷalum' means even thinking, highlighting that mental intent is as significant as the physical act of theft. True virtue requires keeping one's thoughts entirely free from dishonest desires.

ai.literal: Wealth accumulated by theft, exceeding measure, appearing to grow like, will perish.
ai.translation: Wealth accumulated by theft may seem to grow beyond measure, but it will perish utterly.
ai.modern: களவினால் சேர்க்கப்பட்ட செல்வம், எல்லை கடந்து பெருகுவது போலத் தோன்றி, இறுதியில் அழியும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the illusion of wealth acquired through dishonest means or theft. The poet explains that although stolen wealth (களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம்) might appear to grow rapidly and exceed all limits (அளவிறந்து ஆவது போல), this growth is merely a deceptive illusion. In reality, such ill-gotten gains will vanish completely (கெடும்), leaving nothing behind. The key contrast is between the appearance of prosperity and its inevitable, sudden ruin.

ai.literal: The intense desire in theft, in its consequence, will give endless distress.
ai.translation: An intense passion for stealing will, in its ultimate consequence, yield endless distress.
ai.modern: களவு செய்வதில் கொண்டுள்ள மிகுந்த ஆசை, அதன் முடிவில் அழியாத பெரும் துன்பத்தைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against harboring a deep-seated passion for stealing. The word 'கன்றிய' describes a desire that has grown intense, hardened, or obsessive. While theft might promise immediate gain, its ultimate consequence ('விளைவின்கண்') is 'வீயா விழுமம்'—undying, endless misery. The poet emphasizes that the mental inclination towards dishonesty inevitably leads to inescapable ruin.

ai.literal: Desiring grace, being possessors of love, is not with those who watch for forgetfulness desiring wealth.
ai.translation: Being loving and seeking grace is impossible for those who covet others' wealth and watch for their moments of forgetfulness to steal it.
ai.modern: அருளை விரும்பி அன்புடையவராக வாழும் தன்மை, பிறருடைய பொருளைக் கவர எண்ணி அவர்களுடைய மறதியை எதிர்பார்த்துக் காத்திருப்பவர்களிடம் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the incompatibility of compassion and the intent to steal. The word 'poccāppu' refers to the forgetfulness or negligence of others, which thieves look out for as an opportunity. Those who watch for such moments to steal others' wealth ('poruḷ') cannot possess genuine love ('aṉpu') or seek spiritual grace ('aruḷ'). True virtue requires a mind free from the desire to exploit the vulnerability of others.

ai.literal: Within the limits of moderation abiding and living they are incapable of, towards theft intense desire those who have.
ai.translation: Those who harbor an intense desire for stealing are incapable of living their lives within the bounds of moderation and righteousness.
ai.modern: திருடுவதில் மிகுந்த ஆசை கொண்டவர்கள், நேர்மையான அளவுமுறைக்குள் நின்று வாழ இயலாதவர் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights how the desire to steal corrupts a person's ability to live an ethical life. The word 'அளவு' refers to the moral limit or moderation that guides a righteous life, while 'களவு' represents the act of taking what is not given. Those who possess an intense, deep-seated desire ('கன்றிய காதல்') for theft lose their self-restraint. Consequently, they find themselves completely unable ('ஆற்றார்') to conduct their lives ('ஒழுகல்') within the boundaries of honesty and discipline.

ai.literal: The conduct of dark intellect called theft, in those who cherish the power called moderation, exists not.
ai.translation: The practice of dark ignorance called theft will not be found in those who cherish the great power of moderation.
ai.modern: திருட்டு என்று சொல்லப்படும் அறியாமை நிறைந்த செயல், அளவு அறிந்து வாழும் ஆற்றலை விரும்பியவர்களிடம் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the ignorance of theft with the strength of moderation. The author describes theft as 'kār-aṟivāṇmai'—a conduct born of dark, ignorant intellect. On the other hand, knowing and respecting the proper limits of things is described as 'aḷavennum āṟṟal'—the power of moderation. Those who cherish and practice this power of moderation will never harbor the dark desire to steal from others.

ai.literal: Just like virtue stands in the heart of those who know moderation, deceit stands in the heart of those who know theft.
ai.translation: Just as virtue abides in the hearts of those who know the limits of proper conduct, deceit dwells in the minds of those who practice theft.
ai.modern: அளவறிந்து வாழ்பவர்களின் நெஞ்சில் அறம் நிலைத்து நிற்பது போல, திருடத் தெரிந்தவர்களின் நெஞ்சில் வஞ்சகம் நிலைத்து நிற்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet draws a direct parallel between the righteous and the dishonest. Those who understand moderation and live within the limits of virtue (அளவறிந்தார்) will naturally have righteousness (அறம்) firmly established in their hearts. On the other hand, those who are skilled in stealing (களவறிந்தார்) will always have deceit (கரவு) dwelling in their minds. The poet uses the word 'கரவு' (deceit or concealment) to emphasize that a thief's mind is never open or honest; it is constantly occupied with schemes of deception.

ai.literal: Those who do not know other things except theft, having done things beyond measure, will perish right there.
ai.translation: Those who know nothing other than deceitful theft will commit boundless wrongs and perish at that very moment.
ai.modern: திருட்டைத் தவிர வேறு நல்வழிகளை அறியாதவர்கள், நெறிமுறையற்ற செயல்களைச் செய்து அந்த கணத்திலேயே அழிந்து போவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns about the ultimate fate of habitual thieves. Those who do not know or practice any honest means of livelihood other than stealing ('kaḷavu alla maṟṟaiya tēṟṟātavar') will inevitably commit boundless, unlawful acts ('aḷavalla ceytu'). Because they lack moral boundaries, their actions lead to their immediate ruin ('āṅkē vīvar'). The word 'aḷavu' here refers to the limits of righteousness and law, which thieves constantly transgress.

ai.literal: To those who steal, the abode of life will be lost; to those who do not steal, the celestial world will not be denied.
ai.translation: For those who steal, even their very life-abode will be lost; but for those who do not steal, the celestial world of the gods will never be denied.
ai.modern: திருடுபவர்களுக்கு உடம்பாகிய உயிர்நிலை தவறிப்போகும்; திருடாதவர்களுக்குத் தேவர் உலகம் தவறாமல் கிடைக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the ultimate spiritual and physical fates of those who steal and those who practice non-stealing. For the thief, even the basic right to a proper physical existence or the preservation of their life (உயிர்நிலை) is lost due to their actions. In contrast, for those who strictly avoid theft, the ultimate celestial realm of the gods (புத்தேள் உலகு) is guaranteed and will never be withheld from them. The poet uses the contrast between losing one's earthly station and gaining the highest heavenly world to emphasize the gravity of non-stealing.
